newsitem.title: USA: U.S. pork exports to Japan to soar -- U.S. attache.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pork exports to Japan to soar -- U.S. attache.

text.p: U.S. pork exports Japan will soar this year, due to an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in the Taiwan swine herd, according to a recent report from the U.S. agricultural attache in Tokyo.

In a report received Wednesday by the USDA, the attache said U.S. pork exports to Japan could approach 250,000 tonnes in 1997, up from 142,000 tonnes in 1996, with most of the increase being in chilled products.
The following are excerpts from the report:

In the wake of the Ministry of Agriculture's ban on imported pork from Taiwan due to an outbreak of Foot and Mouth Disease(FMD), Japanese pork buyers have been scouring the world in search of new sources of supply.

With Taiwan accounting for more than 40 percent of the 650,000 tons of pork imported into Japan last year, (the embassy) estimates that the import ban will result in more than 200,000 (metric) tons of additional sales for remaining suppliers to the market in 1997. And with domestic production expected to decline by 3 percent this year, Japanese buyers must look overseas to fill the gap.
As the second largest supplier to Japan in 1996, U.S. pork exporters are well-positioned to pick up additional sales.

While it is still unclear exactly how the market will respond to higher prices, which are expected to continue for most of the year, Post is projecting U.S. pork exports to Japan could approach 250,000 tons in 1997, up from 142,000 tons in 1996.

Most of the U.S. export gains in 1997 will be in chilled products as the U.S. accounted for almost half of the 162,000 tons of chilled pork imported in 1996 (with Taiwan accounting for the other half).

Demand for U.S. chilled pork jumped immediately after the FMD outbreak, despite higher prices, with one major U.S. packer reportedly selling out for April deliveries early this week. While loins and tenderloins traditionally account for most U.S. chilled pork sales to Japan, traders are reporting brisk sales of full sets as buyers seek to reduce shortages of additional cuts previously supplied by Taiwan.

U.S. frozen pork exports are also expected to grow, although sales will be slow initially due to high frozen pork stocks (152,000 tons on February 1) and continued high minimum import prices imposed by Japan's pork safeguard policy.
Most sales will occur in the second half of 1997 as the safeguard is scheduled to be lifted July 1, which will reduce the minimum import price by 24 percent to 586.76 yen/kg.
